H1.text: A tea strainer keeps the leaves back. Sea water dries to leave salt.

H2.text: A naphthalene ball in the cupboard shrinks, but never melts.

H3.text: Diya watches her mother strain the tea. Each trick uses one difference.

H5.text: Chemists clean compounds the same way. By the end, you will pick the right trick for any mixture.

P1.text: A chemist makes a new compound. It comes out mixed with junk.

P2.text: Pure means one substance only. So find one property that differs.

P3.text: Turns to vapour? Sublimation. Dissolves better hot? Crystallisation. Different boiling points? Distillation. Prefers another liquid? Extraction. Sticks differently? Chromatography.

B1.text: Start with sublimation. A solid turns straight into vapour, skipping the liquid.

B2.text: Camphor and naphthalene do this. Heat it. The vapour hits a cold surface and turns back into pure solid. Junk stays below.

B3.text: Crystallisation is for solids too. Dissolve the solid in a hot liquid, the solvent.

B4.text: Filter it hot. Then cool it, and pure crystals grow. Impurities stay dissolved.

B5.text: Coloured junk? Activated charcoal soaks it up. Not pure yet? Repeat.

S1.text: Let's run a distillation on our molecule bench. Boil, then cool the vapour back into liquid.

S2.text: In the flask, chloroform and aniline. Chloroform boils at three hundred thirty four kelvin, aniline at four fifty seven.

S3.text: We heat. Chloroform boils first. Its vapour enters the condenser, a tube cooled by water.

S4.text: It turns back into liquid and drips into the receiver. Aniline stays in the flask.

S5.text: Boiling points far apart, one round is enough. This is simple distillation.

D1.text: Boiling points close? Use fractional distillation.

D2.text: A tall fractionating column sits on the flask. The vapour cools and boils again and again, getting purer. Crude oil is split this way.

D3.text: Glycerol breaks down before it boils. So we lower the pressure. Lower pressure, lower boiling point. Soap makers take glycerol from spent lye this way.

D4.text: Now steam distillation. It is for a liquid that does not mix with water, but moves with steam. Like aniline in water.

D5.text: Step one. Each liquid has its own vapour pressure. Aniline's is p one. Water's is p two.

D6.text: Step two. The mixture boils when p one plus p two equals the air pressure, p.

D7.text: Step three. So p one is less than p. Aniline comes over below its own boiling point.

G1.text: Next, differential extraction. The compound is dissolved in water.

G2.text: Add a liquid that does not mix with water, but dissolves the compound better. Shake in a separating funnel.

G3.text: The compound moves into the new layer. Drain the water, then evaporate the solvent.

R2.text: A stationary phase stays still. A mobile phase moves over it.

R3.text: In adsorption chromatography, the still part is silica gel or alumina. What sticks more, moves less. Use a column, or a thin layer on glass.

R4.text: In paper chromatography, water held in the paper is the stationary phase. This is partition chromatography.

R5.text: Watch the plate. The solvent climbs, and each spot climbs at its own speed.

R6.text: R f is the distance moved by the spot, divided by the distance moved by the solvent. Both from the base line.

R7.text: Colourless spots? Use ultraviolet light or iodine vapour. Amino acids show up with ninhydrin.

C1.text: Compare. Chloroform with aniline. They mix, and their boiling points are far apart. Simple distillation.

C2.text: Aniline with water. They do not mix, and aniline moves with steam. Steam distillation.

K1.text: Pause and think. Why not just boil aniline at its own boiling point?

K2.text: It can break down at that heat. With steam, it comes over cooler, and pure.

T1.text: Remember this. Find the one property that differs, and pick the method that uses it.

W1.text: Now, one worked example. These are example figures.

W2.text: The solvent moves ten centimetres from the base line. Spot A moves seven point five, spot B three. Find each R f.

W3.text: Spot A. Seven point five divided by ten. R f is point seven five.

W4.text: Spot B. Three divided by ten. R f is point three.

W5.text: B sticks more to the plate, so it moved less.

X2.text: Students measure from the plate edge, or divide solvent by spot.

X3.text: Measure both from the base line, spot on top. R f is never more than one.

E1.text: Where is this asked? JEE Main has asked to match mixtures with distillation methods. Boards ask about R f.

Q1.text: Exam level now. The solvent front is twelve centimetres from the base line. Spot X has R f point four. Spot Y is three point six centimetres above X. Find the R f of Y. Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is A. Point seven.

A2.text: Spot X moved point four times twelve. Four point eight.

A3.text: Spot Y moved four point eight plus three point six. Eight point four.

A4.text: Eight point four over twelve is point seven. B used only three point six.

Y3.text: Two. Why does steam distillation work below the boiling point?

Y4.text: Three. What is the stationary phase in paper chromatography?
